title: Parvati's tapas
hook: a princess does fierce tapas for Shiva, and a stranger tries to talk her out of it
carry: tapas, study, surrender: the yoga of action

segments.voice: Yesterday: seedless, even the holiest seed let go, and Ramakrishna still came home to his Mother. Today chapter two begins, with a princess on a mountain.

Parvati, daughter of the Himalaya, has set her heart on Shiva, the great ascetic, and Shiva doesn't notice. So she goes up into the mountains and does tapas. In Kalidasa's poem and in the Puranas she sits between fires in the summer heat and in icy water in winter, and eats only leaves that fall by themselves, then not even those. One day a young holy man arrives, polite and curious. Why, he asks, would someone like you burn herself away for Shiva? Ash on his body, snakes for jewelry, a cremation ground for a home.
screen: `SHE SETS HER HEART ON SHIVA.` → `FIRE IN SUMMER, ICE IN WINTER.` → `WHY HIM, OF ALL PEOPLE?`

segments.voice: Parvati defends Shiva and gets up to leave. The stranger stops her and shows his true form: Shiva himself, saying her tapas has won him. That's why she's called Aparna, the one who gave up even leaves, and why women in many regions keep Hartalika Teej, a fast that remembers her tapas, and many Hindus keep Monday fasts for Shiva. Tapas, literally heat, is one of the oldest words in Hinduism, and Patanjali puts it first in sutra 2.1, which opens chapter two: tapah svadhyaya ishvara pranidhanani kriya yogah. Discipline, study and surrender to the Lord are the yoga of action. Kriya means action: yoga you do in daily life. The commentator Vyasa says chapter one spoke to a settled mind, and chapter two to a scattered one. Tapas is the heat of keeping a vow when comfort pulls the other way, and here Vyasa gentles Parvati's extremes: practice it only so far as it doesn't disturb a calm, clear mind. A later commentator adds: or the body's balance. The Gita even counts truthful, kind speech as tapas. Svadhyaya, one's own study: the sacred texts, and, Vyasa adds, repeating om or a mantra. Ishvara pranidhana: offering every action to the Lord and letting go of its fruits, like the Gita's line, whatever you do, eat or give, offer it to me. Sutra 2.2 says why: to cultivate absorption and to thin the afflictions. Thin, the way water wears down stone. Parvati had all three: the heat, the steady remembering of Shiva, and a heart already given.
screen: `HER TAPAS WINS SHIVA.` · `2.1: TAPAS, STUDY, SURRENDER.` · `HEAT THAT DOESN'T HARM.` · then, large: `THINNING THE AFFLICTIONS.`

segments.voice: Try all three in miniature. Tapas: sit still for a few breaths, even when the body wants to shift. Svadhyaya: say one line you love slowly, Om, a mantra or a verse, and really hear it. Surrender: offer this sit to God if you pray, or simply let go of needing it to be good. Then rest on the breath.
Kriya yoga. The yoga of action in sutra 2.1: discipline, study and surrender to the Lord, practiced to cultivate absorption and thin the afflictions.
Your line: tapas, study, surrender, the yoga of action. Parvati's heat, kept gently. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus keep vows such as Monday fasts for Shiva, and in many regions women keep Hartalika Teej in memory of Parvati's tapas; some who follow the Yoga Sutras practice kriya yoga as a daily rhythm of a kept discipline, scripture or mantra, and offering the day's actions to God.

original.note: Sanskrit tapas: heat, discipline, austerity. the first part of kriya yoga.

trapdoor: what you thought: tapas means punishing yourself.
what it means: in Patanjali, the heat of a kept vow, joined with study and surrender, and gentle enough not to disturb a calm mind.
what a scholar hears: Vyasa introduces chapter two as for the vyutthita-chitta, the distracted mind; the phrase kriya yoga is also used by some modern lineages for their own methods, a later usage.
